findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the audit log's datetime ordering
findings.body: The only caller enables this paginator with order_by="-datetime", so self.key is "datetime" and getattr(item, self.key) returns a datetime. get_item_key passes that datetime to math.floor/math.ceil, which raises TypeError for a non-empty page when build_cursor computes next/prev cursors. value_from_cursor also returns the raw cursor integer instead of converting the millisecond timestamp back to a datetime like DateTimePaginator does, so a subsequent page would filter the datetime column against an integer. The optimized audit-log path therefore cannot return a usable first or subsequent page.

findings.title: Negative offsets do not work on Django querysets and will raise AssertionError
findings.body: When enable_advanced_features is true and a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset, this code slices the Django queryset as queryset[negative:stop]. Django explicitly rejects negative queryset indexing with AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported (and stop can itself become negative for sufficiently negative offsets), contrary to the comment claiming the ORM handles it automatically. A privileged user requesting the advertised advanced mode can therefore trigger an unhandled 500 instead of receiving a page; the trimming check at line 891 also compares len(results) with offset+limit+extra even though a negative slice contains limit+extra rows, so the extra-row logic is inconsistent for this branch.

findings.title: BasePaginator change still passes negative offsets for previous-page cursors and affects every paginator user
findings.body: This modifies the shared BasePaginator used by many endpoints, not only audit logs. It clamps negative offsets only when cursor.is_prev is false; a user-controlled cursor such as <value>:-1:1 still reaches queryset[negative:stop] and raises Django's negative-indexing AssertionError. For forward cursors, silently clamping to 0 also changes the contract for all existing paginators and can produce next cursors derived from the original negative offset in build_cursor, risking repeated or inconsistent pages rather than rejecting a malformed cursor.

findings.title: Unconditional dereference of organization_context.member can break previously valid requests
findings.body: organization_context.member is nullable for some authorized principals (for example non-member/token or application-style access that is not a superuser), but this line evaluates organization_context.member.has_global_access on every GET, even when optimized_pagination is not requested. For a non-superuser request with member=None this raises AttributeError and turns a previously working audit-log request into a 500; the check should be guarded or only evaluated when the optimized branch is actually requested.

findings.title: No tests cover the new paginator or optimized audit-log branch
findings.body: The change adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, alters shared BasePaginator slicing, and adds a gated branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, but the PR contains no tests. There is no coverage showing that a datetime-ordered queryset can produce next/prev cursors, that the endpoint gate selects the intended paginator, or what happens for negative, prev, and boundary cursors; those untested cases include the datetime TypeError and negative-slice AssertionError above.

findings.title: Comment claims negative cursor offsets are now safely supported, but no such support is implemented
findings.body: This change only adds a comment; Cursor.__init__ still just does int(offset), exactly as before, and downstream paginators/querysets still reject or mishandle negative offsets. The comment incorrectly suggests a completed, safe behavior change in a shared cursor type and may lead future callers to rely on negative offsets that currently cause errors.
